summary:
A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map lists Rhode Island among its 'Most Protective' states for gender-identity nondiscrimination. The same map reports erosion at the federal layer and concludes that its top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so the ranking describes Rhode Island's own statute rather than conditions a visitor will meet at every point of the journey.

Discrimination based on gender identity or expression has been unlawful in Rhode Island since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations under R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 28-5-3, 28-5-7, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.3 and 11-24-2. A bill signed in June 2023 added explicit bans covering patient care, nursing and related healthcare, and the long-standing housing exemption for dwellings with three occupants or fewer was repealed with effect from 1 January 2023.

Rhode Island hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity or expression, with the gender-identity coverage placed in statute at R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-28-46. The gay and trans panic defense was repealed in June 2018 by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo the following month and effective immediately.

Identity documents are changeable on a self-declaration-plus-clinical-confirmation basis rather than a surgical one. Since 23 October 2014 a birth certificate gender change has required a Birth Certificate Request Form together with an affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status, replacing the earlier sex reassignment surgery requirement. The Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's licence on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. A third gender marker, X, was announced for driver's licences and birth certificates in August 2019 with availability from July 2020, and a June 2018 law requires transgender people to be recorded correctly on death certificates.

Single-occupancy toilets may be designated gender-neutral with effect from 1 January 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021. Rhode Island also appears on the transgender healthcare equality map among jurisdictions covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches, which are drafted to make those protections enforceable against out-of-state action.

In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League revised its transgender athletes policy. Transgender athletes remain able to compete, but member schools now carry responsibility for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when they determine gender-based eligibility, replacing the prior rule that allowed participation consistent with gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment map that ranks Rhode Island in its top tier also records federal-layer erosion, including the District of Columbia House bathroom ban, and states plainly that the top tier can no longer be treated as the most protective tier nationwide. A visitor's exposure at airports, federal buildings and border processing therefore does not track Rhode Island's state-law position.

Rhode Island's nondiscrimination statutes have protected sexual orientation since 1995 on the same terms as gender identity, in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations, with the June 2023 healthcare additions and the 1 January 2023 repeal of the small-dwelling housing exemption applying to both characteristics. Hate-crime penalty enhancements likewise cover actual or perceived sexual orientation, and the gay panic defense was repealed on the same 2018 votes.

The state's conversion therapy prohibition on minors, signed 19 July 2017 after House votes of 69-0 and 62-0 and a Senate vote of 29-0, and its anti-bullying statute covering sexual orientation, cyberbullying and harassment across all public schools, sit alongside the gender-identity protections rather than adding separate visitor-facing exposure.
localsOnly:
Residents have access to a documented route for aligning identity records: a birth certificate gender change on a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant affidavit confirming transgender status since 23 October 2014, a corrected driver's licence on a signed Gender Designation Form, the X marker available on licences and birth certificates from July 2020, and correct recording on death certificates under the June 2018 law.

State law bars discrimination on gender identity or expression in employment, credit, housing, public accommodations and, since June 2023, in patient care, nursing and related healthcare, with hate-crime enhancements for gender-identity-motivated offences and the panic defense unavailable as a defense since 2018. Shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches are listed for Rhode Island on the transgender healthcare equality map and are described as enforceable against out-of-state action.

Conversion therapy on minors and state funding for it have been prohibited since 19 July 2017. The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of sexual orientation, expressly covers cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all public schools.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no enforcement data for Rhode Island's gender-identity nondiscrimination provisions: no complaint volumes, no outcomes, and no evidence on how the statutes are applied in practice against a visitor rather than a resident.

No incident of anti-trans violence in Rhode Island is documented in this inventory, and no dated prevalence figure for the state is available, so the record supports no statement about the current level of such violence either way.

The scope of the Rhode Island shield-law listing is unresolved here: the inventory identifies the 2023 and 2024 batches and their out-of-state reach but does not set out which specific protections the state's measures carry, nor how they would apply to a visitor seeking care.

How Rhode Island-issued credentials interact with the federal document and entry rules described in the parent record is not sourced at this level, and neither is facility access in privately operated venues, which the single-occupancy toilet provision does not address.

The March 2025 Interscholastic League revision is stated as policy text; no documented case of its application, and no later revision, appears in the inventory.
